GLEASON–KAHANE– ˙ZELAZKO THEOREMS IN
FUNCTION SPACES
JAVAD MASHREGHI AND THOMAS RANSFORD
Abstract. The Gleason–Kahane–˙Zelazko theorem states that a
linear functional on a Banach algebra that is non-zero on invertible
elements is necessarily a scalar multiple of a character. Recently
this theorem has been extended to certain Banach function spaces
that are not algebras. In this article we present a brief survey of
these extensions.
1. Introduction
The following result is known as the Gleason–Kahane– ˙Zelazko the-
orem (or GKZ-theorem for short). For commutative algebras it was
proved independently by Gleason [8] and by Kahane and ˙Zelazko [10].
Subsequently ˙Zelazko [19] extended it to the non-commutative case.
Theorem 1.1. Let A be a complex unital Banach algebra, and let
Λ : A →C be a linear functional such that Λ(1) = 1 and Λ(a) ̸= 0 for
all invertible elements a ∈A. Then Λ(ab) = Λ(a)Λ(b) for all a, b ∈A.
Note that continuity of Λ is not assumed. This result is thus an early
example of an automatic continuity theorem.
The original proofs of Theorem 1.1 used results about entire func-
tions. In §2 we include a completely elementary proof, due to Roitman
and Sternfeld, which we believe deserves to be more widely known.
The GKZ-theorem has been extended in many diﬀerent ways; see
for example the article of Jarosz [9]. Here we present a short survey of
some recent extensions of the theorem to function spaces. The starting
point is a generalization of the GKZ-theorem to A-modules, whose
details are described in §3. The module theorem leads to versions of

3. A GKZ-theorem for modules
The following result, which is a generalization of classical GKZ-
theorem to modules, was obtained in [12].
Theorem 3.1. Let A be a complex unital Banach algebra, let M be
a left A-module, and let S be a non-empty subset of M satisfying the
following conditions:
(S1) S generates M as an A-module;
(S2) if a ∈A is invertible and s ∈S, then as ∈S;
(S3) if s1, s2 ∈S, then there exist a1, a2 ∈A such that a1S ∪a2S ⊂S
and a1s1 = a2s2.
Let Λ : M →C be a linear functional such that Λ(s) ̸= 0 for all s ∈S.
Then there exists a unique character χ on A such that
(3)
Λ(am) = χ(a)Λ(m)
(a ∈A, m ∈M).
Notice that continuity of Λ is not assumed. Indeed, the A-module
M is not assumed to carry any topological structure.
Theorem 3.1 contains the classical GKZ-theorem as a special case, as
can be seen by taking M = A and S to be the set of invertible elements
of A. Note, however, that the GKZ-theorem is used in its proof.
Proof. Uniqueness of χ is clear. Indeed, ﬁxing any s ∈S, by (3) we
must have
χ(a) = Λ(as)/Λ(s)
(a ∈A).
To prove existence, we begin by deriving inspiration from this last
equation. Given s ∈S, deﬁne χs : A →C by
χs(a) := Λ(as)/Λ(s)
(a ∈A).
Clearly χs is a linear functional on A satisfying χs(1) = 1, and from
property (S2) we have χs(a) ̸= 0 for all invertible a ∈A. By Theo-
rem 1.1, it follows that χs is a character on A.
Next, given s1, s2 ∈S, property (S3) yields the existence of elements
a1, a2 ∈A such that a1S ∪a2S ⊂S and a1s1 = a2s2. Then Λ(a1s1) =
Λ(a2s2), whence
(4)
χs1(a1)Λ(s1) = χs2(a2)Λ(s2).
Equally, for each a ∈A, we have aa1s1 = aa2s2, whence
(5)
χs1(aa1)Λ(s1) = χs2(aa2)Λ(s2).
Now both sides of (4) are non-zero, because ajsj ∈S. Thus we may
divide (5) by (4) to obtain
χs1(a) = χs2(a).

The following theorem, ﬁrst obtained in [12], is an analogue of the
GKZ-theorem for Hardy spaces.
Theorem 4.1. Let 0 < p ≤∞and let Λ : Hp →C be a linear
functional such that Λ(1) = 1 and Λ(g) ̸= 0 for all outer functions
g ∈Hp. Then there exists w ∈D such that
Λ(f) = f(w)
(f ∈Hp).
Note that, once again, continuity of Λ is not assumed.
Proof. We apply Theorem 3.1 with M := Hp and A := H∞, taking S
to be the set of outer functions in Hp.
Property (S1) holds by the inner-outer factorization theorem for Hp.
Property (S2) holds because every invertible function in h ∈H∞is
outer. Indeed, multiplying together the inner-outer factorizations of h
and 1/h, we obtain a factorization of 1, and by uniqueness it follows
that the inner factors of h and 1/h must both be unimodular constants.
Property (S3) holds because every outer function can be represented
as the quotient of two bounded outer functions [5, Proof of Theo-
rem 2.1].
Thus, by Theorem 3.1, there exists a character χ on H∞such that

To ﬁnish the proof, we show that Λ(f) = f(w) for all f ∈Hp. Given

As an application of Theorem 4.1, we obtain the following very simple
characterization of weighted composition operators on Hardy spaces.
Corollary 4.2. Let 0 < p ≤∞and let T : Hp →Hol(D) be a linear
map such that (Tg)(z) ̸= 0 for all outer functions g ∈Hp and all z ∈D.
Then there exist holomorphic functions φ : D →D and ψ : D →C\{0}
such that
Tf = ψ.(f ◦φ)
(f ∈Hp).
Proof. Set ψ := T1.
This is a holomorphic function on D, and is
nowhere zero because 1 is outer. Deﬁne φ := (Tu)/ψ, where u(z) := z.
This too is a holomorphic function on D.
Fix z ∈D. The map f 7→(Tf)(z)/ψ(z) is a linear functional on Hp
that sends 1 to 1 and is non-zero on outer functions. By Theorem 4.1,
there exists w ∈D such that (Tf)(z)/ψ(z) = f(w) for all f ∈Hp.
Taking f := u, we see that w = φ(z). Thus φ(z) ∈D and (Tf)(z) =
ψ(z)f(φ(z)) for all f ∈Hp.
□
5. Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
The results in the previous section depend heavily on the inner-
outer factorization in Hardy spaces.
If we want to extend them to
other function spaces using the same basic method, then we need to
establish analogous factorization theorems for these spaces. In general
this is diﬃcult. But there is one family of spaces where, thanks to some
recent developments, it is possible. The family in question is a certain
class of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. In this section we describe
the background leading to the factorization theorem, and in the next
section we apply it to deduce a GKZ-theorem for Dirichlet spaces.
Let Ωbe a set. A reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) on Ωis a
Hilbert space H of complex-valued functions on Ωsuch that, for each
t ∈Ω, the evaluation functional f 7→f(t) : H →C is continuous.
Let H be a RKHS on Ω. By the Riesz representation theorem, given
t ∈Ω, there exists a unique kt ∈H such that
f(t) = ⟨f, kt⟩
(f ∈H).
The function kt is called the reproducing kernel for the point t. The
function K : Ω× Ω→C deﬁned by K(s, t) := kt(s) = ⟨kt, ks⟩H is
called the reproducing kernel for H.
A multiplier for H is a function h : Ω→C such that hf ∈H for
all f ∈H. By the closed graph theorem, f 7→hf is then a bounded
operator on H. The set of multipliers is denoted M(H). It is a Banach
algebra with respect to the multiplier norm, deﬁned by
∥h∥M(H) := sup{∥hf∥H : ∥f∥H ≤1}.

For general background on RKHS’s we refer to the book [14], and for
more information on the complete Pick property we recommend [1].
Now we can state the promised factorization theorem. It is due to
to Aleman, Hartz, McCarthy and Richter [3, Theorem 1].
Theorem 5.1. Let H be an RKHS on Ω.
Assume that H has the
complete Pick property. Then each f ∈H can be factorized as f = h/k,
where h, k ∈M(H) and k is nowhere-zero on Ω.
Examples of RKHS’s with the complete Pick property include the
Hardy space H2 and the Dirichlet space D. On the other hand, the
Bergman space A2 := L2(D) ∩Hol(D) is an RKHS without the com-
plete Pick property, and in fact Theorem 5.1 fails for A2. Indeed, the
multiplier algebra of A2 is H∞, but not every function f ∈A2 can be
written as h/k with h, k ∈H∞, because h/k has radial limits a.e. on T,
yet there exist f ∈A2 without any radial limits at all (see [4] for a very
simple example).

The following result, obtained in [11], is an analogue of the GKZ-
theorem for Dirichlet spaces.
Theorem 6.1. Let ω be a positive superharmonic function on D. Let
Λ : Dω →C be a linear functional such that Λ(1) = 1 and Λ(g) ̸= 0 for
all nowhere-vanishing functions g ∈Dω. Then there exists w ∈D such
that Λ(f) = f(w) for all f ∈Dω.
Proof. We apply Theorem 3.1, taking M to be Dω and A = M(Dω),
the multiplier algebra of Dω. Let S be the set of nowhere-vanishing
functions in Dω. We need to check the conditions (S1), (S2) and (S3)
of Theorem 3.1.
For condition (S1), it suﬃces to show that every f ∈Dω can be
written as f = g1 + g2, where g1, g2 ∈Dω and neither function gj has
a zero in D. Given f ∈Dw, factor it as f = hg, where h is inner and
g outer. By [2, Chapter IV, Theorem 3.4], we have g ∈Dw. Then
f = (h−2)g +2g is the sum of two nowhere-vanishing functions in Dw.
Thus condition (1) is veriﬁed.
Condition (S2) is obviously satisﬁed, since invertible elements of
M(D) must be everywhere non-zero on D.
For condition (S3), let g1, g2 be nowhere-vanishing elements of Dω.
By a theorem of Shimorin [18], the space Dω is a RKHS with the
complete Pick property. Therefore, by Theorem 5.1, we can write gj =

Set a1 := h2k1 and a2 := h1k2. These a1, a2 are nowhere-vanishing
elements of M(Dω), so ajS ∪a2S ⊂S, and further a1g1 = a2g2. Thus
condition (S3) is satisﬁed.
By Theorem 3.1, there exists a character χ on M(Dω) such that

(f ∈D, h ∈M(Dω)).

7. GKZ-theorems in other function spaces
The proofs of Theorems 4.1 and 6.1 use special factorization proper-
ties of Hardy spaces and Dirichlet spaces, and do not easily generalize
to other families of spaces. However, if we are willing to assume the
continuity of the linear maps involved, then these theorems do extend
to a wide variety of other spaces, albeit with a diﬀerent proof.
In what follows, we shall consider a Banach space X ⊂Hol(D) with
the following properties:
(X1) for each w ∈D, the map f 7→f(w) : X →C is continuous;
(X2) X contains the polynomials and they are dense in X;
(X3) X is shift-invariant: f ∈X ⇒zf ∈X.
We write M(X) for the multiplier algebra of X, namely
M(X) := {h ∈Hol(D) : hf ∈X for all f ∈X},
∥h∥M(X) := sup{∥hf∥X : ∥f∥X ≤1}.
Using property (X1) above, it is not hard to see that M(X) can be iden-
tiﬁed with a closed subalgebra of the algebra of all bounded linear op-
erators on X, so it is a Banach algebra. For each w ∈D, the evaluation
functional h 7→h(w) is a character on M(X), so |h(w)| ≤∥h∥M(X). It
follows that M(X) ⊂H∞. As X contains the constants, we also have
M(X) ⊂X.
We also consider a subset Y of X with the following properties:
(Y1) if g ∈X and 0 < infD |g| ≤supD |g| < ∞, then g ∈Y ;
(Y2) if g(z) := z −λ where λ ∈T, then g ∈Y .
Examples of spaces X satisfying (X1)–(X3) include:
• the Hardy spaces Hp (1 ≤p < ∞);
• the Bergman spaces Ap (1 ≤p < ∞);
• the holomorphic Besov spaces Bp (1 ≤p < ∞);
• the superharmonically weighted Dirichlet spaces Dω;
• the Sobolev spaces Sp := {f : f ′ ∈Hp} (1 ≤p < ∞);
• the disk algebra A(D);
• the little Bloch space B0;
• the space VMOA of functions of vanishing mean oscillation;
• the de Branges–Rovnyak spaces H(b), for non-extreme points b
in the unit ball of H∞.
Examples of sets Y satisfying (Y1)–(Y2) include:

8. Open problems
The results in this short survey lead to open problems in other ﬁelds.
We give two examples.
In Theorem 7.1, we assumed the continuity of the linear functional Λ.
This naturally raises a question about automatic continuity.
Problem 8.1. Let X, Y be as in Theorem 7.1 and let Λ : X →C be a
linear functional such that Λ(g) ̸= 0 for all g ∈Y . Is Λ automatically
continuous?
Thanks to Theorems 4.1 and 6.1, we know that the answer is yes if
(X, Y ) = (Hp, outer functions) or (X, Y ) = (Dω, non-zero functions).
However, the proofs use special properties of these spaces. Is there is
an abstract automatic continuity argument that takes care of general
(X, Y )?
The proof of Theorem 6.1 used two factorization properties of Dω,
namely, every f ∈Dω can be written as
• f = h/k, where h, k ∈M(Dω), and
• f = bg, where b is bounded and g ∈Dω is zero-free.
The ﬁrst of these is a consequence of a general theorem about RKHS’s
(Theorem 5.1). However, the second appears to make use of special
properties of Dirichlet spaces.
This prompts the following series of
questions.
Problem 8.2. Let H be a RKHS with the complete Pick property, and
let f ∈H.
(1) Can we write f = bg, where b is bounded and g ∈H is zero-free?
(2) Can we write f = hg, where h ∈M(H) and g ∈H is zero-free?
(3) Can we write f = hg, where h ∈M(H) and g ∈H is cyclic?
(To say that g is cyclic means that M(H)g = H.)
An aﬃrmative answer to (2) or (3) would likely have applications in
other ﬁelds.

Abstract: The Gleason–Kahane–˙Zelazko theorem states that a linear functional on a Banach algebra that is non-zero on invertible elements is necessarily a scalar multiple of a character. Recently this theorem has been extended to certain Banach function spaces that are not algebras. In this article we present a brief survey of these extensions.
